definition: Showy, inflated language that sounds impressive but says very little.
example: The novel's villain hides his ignorance behind a wall of bombast and borrowed quotations.
nuance: Eloquence is fluent speech that actually persuades; bombast only puffs itself up, and the word is always a criticism.
prompt: A guest speaker addresses a school's graduating class at the end of the year.
options: Beneath the speaker's bombast about 'limitless horizons,' graduates heard little real advice.
The speaker's bombast was so plain and brief that her whole talk fit neatly on a single index card.
Grateful graduates praised the bombast of her quiet, modest, and carefully reasoned advice about budgeting.
The bombast of the fireworks rattled the gym windows as the families left the ceremony.
reasons: Grand phrases that leave listeners with nothing useful are exactly what this word describes.
Short, plain speech is the reverse of puffed-up, overblown language.
The word is a criticism of empty showiness, so it cannot praise modest, careful reasoning.
This confuses the word with a loud blast; it refers to inflated words, not noise.

practice.prompt: A company writes a brochure to advertise its new kitchen blender.
options: Customers sent the company a bombast of angry emails after several blenders began leaking from the base.
Shoppers trusted the brochure because its bombast was so honest, modest, and free of exaggeration.
The brochure's bombast called the blender 'a culinary revolution,' though it only made smoothies.
The brochure listed the blender's wattage and speeds with admirable bombast, in two short, factual lines.
reasons: This mixes the word up with bombardment; it does not mean a flood of messages.
Exaggeration is the heart of the word, so honest, modest writing cannot be described this way.
Lofty claims wildly out of proportion to an ordinary product show inflated, hollow language.
Brief factual lines lack the overblown style the word requires, and it is never admirable.
